card.hook: Here's the odd thing about Victoria Peak: the very top is closed to visitors, yet the view that fills your phone from the paths around it is the one everyone remembers. Towers, harbour and islands all fit in one frame.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near 盧吉道, about 420 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and you'll have the Peak's slopes and the nearby buildings in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of harbour and skyline, then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the towers of Central or a far-off island.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, because the straight line of the water shows any tilt.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is worth a try, as the light softens and the city lights come on. If it's properly dark, use night mode and rest your phone on something solid. If the view is hazy, wait a little.
card.selfie_here: Walk to Lugard Road Lookout on the Peak Circular Walk, a short, flat walk from Peak Tower. Many people stop too early, so keep going until the lookout. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the city open up behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The summit is closed to the public, so take your photos from the public areas around it. If you wander off the main paths, put safety first.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole skyline, then zoom in and see if you can pick out Lamma Island.
card.good_to_know: At 552 metres, Victoria Peak is the tallest hill on Hong Kong Island, and locals just call it The Peak. A governor's summer house went up here around 1868, and the Peak Tram opened in 1888, making the climb much easier. The summit now carries a radio facility.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon near 盧吉道, about 420 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and you'll have the Peak's slopes and the nearby buildings in front of you.

card.hook: Most people shuffle down Temple Street with their eyes on the snacks and miss the best bit. Stop where the market splits around the Tin Hau temple and you get old roof tiles, hanging incense coils and neon stalls all in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of the Tin Hau temple on Temple Street, where the stalls split around the temple complex. Face the temple so the ornate roof and the incense coils are ahead of you, with the market and fortune-teller stalls on either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the roof and the stalls beside it. Switch to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the incense coils without stepping into anyone's way.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the temple roof on the upper line, then tap the brightest part of the screen and slide it a little darker so the neon doesn't blow out.
card.best_time: Dusk is the sweet spot. The lights come on and the market gets lively, so arrive then and keep shooting as it gets darker. It's usually crowded around dusk, so be patient.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the red archway at the market entrance, which several guides call the market's signature backdrop. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and let the arch and the lit stalls fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little way back along Temple Street, away from the archway, while you stand beneath it, so the whole arch and the market lanes fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The street gets busy, so keep to the edge of the walkway when you stop to shoot. The temple is a place of worship, so be respectful around it.
card.challenge: Can you get the temple roof, a curl of incense and a glowing stall sign all in one shot? Bonus points if nobody's elbow sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: Temple Street was built in the Qing dynasty and is named after the Tin Hau temple on the site. It's one of the busiest night markets in Hong Kong, with more than a hundred stalls full of colourful lights. Locals and visitors both love it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right in front of the Tin Hau temple on Temple Street, where the stalls split around the temple complex. Face the temple so the ornate roof and the incense coils are ahead of you, with the market and fortune-teller stalls on either side.

card.hook: The street corner outside The Peninsula is all traffic and crowds, and everyone's holding their phone up at the same angle. Step into the garden and the hotel peeks out through the branches instead.
card.stand_here: Stand in Salisbury Road Garden, the garden on Salisbury Road, and look back at the hotel. It's to the south-west of you, so face south-west and shoot through the trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hotel and the trees around it. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the facade closer while the branches still frame it. Use zoom 0.5x only if you move closer to the frontage, and hold the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hotel, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the bright facade keeps its detail, and switch on the gridlines to keep the building straight.
card.best_time: If you can visit in the weeks before Christmas, the hotel's festive decorations are traditionally up by then, so the street-level views look quite different. Check what's up on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the hotel forecourt on the Salisbury Road frontage, where a red taxi makes a popular photo prop. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you want more of the building, and keep the hotel over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: At street level, use the pavements and crossings, and don't step into barriered areas or stand near traffic. The garden and pavements are public, but the hotel itself is private, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Take three frames at different zooms, with a branch framing one side of each, and pick the one where the building looks perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: The Peninsula opened on 11 December 1928 at the corner of Nathan Road and Salisbury Road. In 1994 a 30-storey tower was added in a similar style, and the original front facade and forecourt were kept. The hotel is also known for its fleet of Rolls-Royces painted in its own green.

card.hook: The best view of Hong Kong's second-tallest building is from the other side of the harbour, so you get a ferry-ride-sized stretch of water between you and a 412-metre tower. That open water is what makes it so easy to frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade on the Kowloon waterfront and face across Victoria Harbour to Hong Kong Island. Two IFC is across the water to the south-west, in the right-hand part of your frame, with the Central skyline and the Observation Wheel close by.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole skyline and the harbour. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Zoom 0.5x makes the tower look tiny, so save it for the promenade itself or the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line so the tower gets most of the frame, and keep a strip of harbour water at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good choice. Once the lights come on, switch to night mode and hold still for the few seconds it needs.
card.selfie_here: Try the open-air Roof Garden at IFC Mall (8 Finance Street), which has sofas and tables for public use. Use the front camera, go to zoom 0.5x and get the harbour and skyscrapers behind your shoulder. We couldn't confirm that Two IFC sits right behind you there, so check your screen before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Near IFC, try the footbridge over Connaught Road Central: ask a passer-by to stand on or near it and frame you with the tower behind, but check the map first because we haven't confirmed the exact spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is an open public waterfront, but check the official site for closures or works before you go. The office towers are private, so enjoy them from outside.
card.challenge: Find the Observation Wheel beside the Central skyline and squeeze it into the same shot as the twin towers.
card.good_to_know: Two IFC was completed on 18 October 2003 and is the taller twin at 412 metres, next to One IFC at 210 metres. It's quoted as having 88 storeys, a lucky number in Cantonese culture, though floors like the 14th and 24th are left out. You might spot the towers in films too, including The Dark Knight.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade on the Kowloon waterfront and face across Victoria Harbour to Hong Kong Island. Two IFC is across the water to the south-west, in the right-hand part of your frame, with the Central skyline and the Observation Wheel close by.

card.hook: Picture a bronze Bruce Lee mid-pose, and behind you the whole Hong Kong Island skyline lined up across the water like it's waiting for its close-up. Most people rush to the statue, but the railing is the sneaky star of this walk.
card.stand_here: Stand at the central railings between the Bruce Lee statue and the west seating areas on the Avenue of Stars. Face across Victoria Harbour to the Hong Kong Island skyline, where you can pick out IFC and Bank of China Tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full skyline and the railing, then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. On many phones, zoom 2x to 5x will pull in the Central towers for a tighter shot. For a second picture, turn round and frame the Bruce Lee statue with a little of the city behind him.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line so the skyline sits above the railing, and let the railing lead the eye into the picture.
card.best_time: Go at sunset and blue hour, before the Symphony of Lights show at about 8 pm. Arrive early to get a clear spot at the railing, and use night mode once it's dark. The show schedule can change and the show is cancelled in severe weather, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze Bruce Lee statue near the middle of the promenade with the harbour behind you, so Victoria Harbour and the skyline fill the background. Use the front camera, and if yours has a 0.5x button, tap it to fit more of the view over your shoulder. For something sillier, the McDull cartoon-pig statue at the far end of the promenade makes a playful backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on or damage the plaques and sculptures while you pose.
card.challenge: Can you get yourself, Bruce Lee and the IFC tower all in one picture without anyone's head getting in the way?
card.good_to_know: The Avenue of Stars is about 440 metres long and was modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, honouring people from Hong Kong's film industry. It opened on 28 April 2004 and reopened on 31 January 2019 after three years of renovation. The bronze Bruce Lee is 2.5 metres tall and was added in 2005, and he may stand in a different spot from where older photos show him.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the central railings between the Bruce Lee statue and the west seating areas on the Avenue of Stars. Face across Victoria Harbour to the Hong Kong Island skyline, where you can pick out IFC and Bank of China Tower.

card.hook: Picture an old temple with glass towers peeking over its roof and the buzz of Hollywood Road right outside its doors. That clash of old and busy is exactly why you'll want your phone out here.
card.stand_here: Head for Man Mo Temple at 124-126 Hollywood Road in Sheung Wan. The phone icon sits at the centre of the temple outline, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Stand on the street or in the courtyard facing the front of the temple.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the façade and some street in the shot, then switch to 1x for most photos. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for carvings and lanterns you can't get close to.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line them up with the temple's upright edges so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Aim for earlier in the day, when it's usually less crowded and you can take your time. Daylight is best for the outside, and if it's dim inside, let night mode do its thing.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement at the temple's front entrance, 124-126 Hollywood Road, with the carved entrance behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if yours has it) and hold it a bit low so the stone lions, wooden doors and carved panels show up over your shoulder, with the high-rises above.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Hollywood Road facing the entrance while you stand in front of it, and ask them to use zoom 0.5x so you and the façade both fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Turn your flash off, especially near worshippers and altars, and follow any no-photo signs. The incense smoke is intense and can irritate your throat after about 10 minutes, so bring a light scarf and take breaks outside.
card.challenge: Get three shots: one wide with the street in it, one medium of the entrance, and one close-up of a carving or a lantern. Bonus points if there's incense smoke drifting through the light.
card.good_to_know: Man Mo Temple was built in 1847 and is dedicated to Man Cheong, the god of literature, and Kwan Tai, the martial god. Students once came here to ask for help with the imperial exams. It's a Grade I historic building and a declared monument, and it's part of a trio with Lit Shing Temple and Kung So, the old assembly hall.

card.hook: A green-and-white ferry slides up to the pier with the whole Hong Kong Island skyline lined up behind it, and you barely have to try. It's a ready-made postcard, so be patient and let the boat come to you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the steps beside the 1915 Clock Tower, next to the Star Ferry pier at Tsim Sha Tsui. Face the harbour, looking down at the boats as they dock, with the Hong Kong Island skyline across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the ferry, the pier and the skyline together. Go to 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single boat against the buildings, or 0.5x to squeeze the clock tower and the pier into one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the ferry, then slide the picture a little darker if the sky is bright so the buildings keep their detail, and use the gridlines to keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Check the sunset time and the ferry timetable on the day, because both can vary. Then pick a moment when a boat is just arriving.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps next to the 1915 Clock Tower, beside the pier entrance. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the clock tower or the pier over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine on the ferry crossing, from both decks. Keep your bags out of the way and don't block the walkway while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Take a burst or a Live Photo as the boat docks, then pick the frame where the ferry sits perfectly in front of the tallest building.
card.good_to_know: The Star Ferry is the green-and-white passenger ferry that crosses Victoria Harbour. Its Tsim Sha Tsui pier is on the Kowloon side, and the 1915 Clock Tower stands right beside it. For a higher view looking down on the ferry as it comes in, try the Ocean Terminal Deck.

card.hook: Some people look at this tower and see a meat cleaver, and once you've seen it, you can't unsee it. Locals even call it 'one knife'.
card.stand_here: Stand in Statue Square, an open plaza just a short walk (about 3 minutes) from the tower. Face the tower, which is to the south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower with the skyline around it. If the top gets chopped off, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the glass and triangle pattern near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up on an upright grid line, and leave a little sky above the masts.
card.best_time: In daylight, the glass and sharp angles give you strong lines and reflections against the Central skyline. After dark the lit tower looks striking, especially from Garden Road or across the water at Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade.
card.selfie_here: Try the open plaza at the base of the tower at 1 Garden Road. Turn your back to the tower, use the front camera, and let it rise behind your shoulder. Switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, so more of the tower fits in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Statue Square plaza while you stand in front of them, with the full tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is a working bank headquarters. Check the official site before you plan to go inside, and don't count on the 43rd-floor observation deck, as it isn't a reliable option now.
card.challenge: Walk around the tower and see how its outline changes. Can you catch the 'one knife' from your best angle?
card.good_to_know: I. M. Pei designed the Bank of China Tower, and it was finished in 1990. It's 315 m tall, or 367.4 m with its two masts, and it was the tallest building in Asia from 1990 to 1992. Its triangular frameworks under glass walls are why the shape seems to change as you move.

card.hook: Picture this: office workers glide uphill, walkers overtake on the moving walkways, and bars and shopfronts slide past on both sides. This escalator is real city life, not a staged view, and that's why your photo will feel alive.
card.stand_here: Stand on Staunton Street in SoHo, where the escalator passes beside you at street level. The main escalator lies to the north-east of this point, so face that way and wait for a walker to pass alongside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit a walker beside the escalator with the SoHo shopfronts around them. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it to pick out one person without stepping into the flow. In narrow spots like Shelley Street, zoom 0.5x fits the whole stepped street and roof in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the escalator along one third of the frame and the walker where two lines cross, then tap the walker and drag the brightness down a touch if the street behind looks washed out.
card.best_time: The roof is partly translucent, so the light under it is soft and kind to faces. The escalator runs downhill in the early morning and uphill from 10 a.m., so choose the direction you want. Check the official site for current hours and direction before you go.
card.selfie_here: Ride to the middle of the escalator, turn around, and shoot with the front camera so Central's street scene unfolds behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of the view. One of the guides we found was a bit garbled on this tip, so treat it as a fun try rather than a sure thing.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on one of the footbridges that cross the escalator corridor and frame you on the moving walkway below.
card.rules_and_safety: Stand on the right and leave the left free for people walking past. Don't stop right in front of the escalator entrance for selfies, and keep yourself and any selfie stick out of the foot traffic. Brace against the handrail, since the escalator is moving.
card.challenge: Get the escalator running through your shot like a line, add exactly one person for scale, and wait for a clear gap with no photobombers.
card.good_to_know: The Central–Mid-Levels escalator is about 800 m long and climbs more than 135 m, which makes it the second longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. It opened on 15 October 1993 and has 18 escalators and three moving walkways. It also helped turn the streets alongside it into the SoHo restaurant and bar district.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Staunton Street in SoHo, where the escalator passes beside you at street level. The main escalator lies to the north-east of this point, so face that way and wait for a walker to pass alongside it.

card.hook: Most people queue for the Peak Tram. You get to stand underneath it instead, watching a little green tram slide across the hillside above red taxis. Not bad for a spot with very few tourists.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kennedy Road, at the Kennedy Road Peak Tram station, where the tram runs overhead. Face up at the tram slanting above the road. The line climbs the slope to the south-west of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the tram and the street together. Try 0.5x if you want more of the structure above your head, or 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a close-up of the tram car.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tram's diagonal up along one of them, with the road filling the bottom of the picture.
card.best_time: Go in daylight so you can see the tram's green. If it's cloudy, this halfway-up spot is a better bet than the summit, which can be stuck in cloud.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stone bridge at the MacDonnell Road tram stop, which looks over the slope the tram climbs. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the bridge, the greenery and the climbing tram behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Along Barker Road, hand your phone to a passer-by and stand where the tram can be seen behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flying drones on the property of the Peak Tram and Peak Tower is prohibited without the management company's permission. Check the official site before you go to see how the stops are running.
card.challenge: Get the tram and a taxi in the same frame. Turn on Live Photos, then pick your best moment afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The Peak Tram has carried people from Central up to Victoria Peak since 1888, and it was the first funicular in Asia. The line runs about 1.4 kilometres and climbs just under 400 metres. It reopened on 27 August 2022 after a long renovation.

card.hook: Picture a tropical bird on a branch, with a glass office tower rising behind it. That's Hong Kong Park, a patch of green tucked right into Central's skyscrapers. The birds won't pose, so give them a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Edward Youde Aviary, inside the park near the pond and pavilions. The middle of the park is about 150 m to the north-east of the aviary, about 2 minutes on foot. Face the birds, with the pavilions and trees behind them.
card.zoom: Use zoom 2x-5x for birds, depending on your phone. Switch to zoom 1x for wider shots of the aviary and pavilions, and zoom 0.5x at the lake to fit the waterfall and towers into one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bird, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) if the sky behind it is bright, and switch on the gridlines to keep the towers straight.
card.best_time: Pick a dry day, when the park is usually quieter. Check where the light falls on the lake and towers before you set up.
card.selfie_here: Head to the edge of the central pond at the Artificial Lake, by the fountain, with the lily pads in view. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it out so the Central skyscrapers rise over your shoulder. The pond adds reflections, so you get the park and the skyline in one go.
card.rules_and_safety: The aviary is described as free to enter, but some areas may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for one bird to settle on a branch, then catch it with a tower blurred behind it, and see if you can do it in three tries.
card.good_to_know: Hong Kong Park opened on 23 May 1991 and covers about 8 hectares. The site was once part of the Victoria Barracks, and a few of the old buildings are still there. Flagstaff House, dating from 1846, is now a teaware museum. The Edward Youde Aviary is the largest aviary in Hong Kong.

card.hook: Walk in off Hollywood Road and the noise of Central just drops away. In front of you is a wide, open yard with a big red-brick Victorian building filling the view, and it used to be a police station.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Parade Ground, in the middle of the open ground. Face the red-brick Barrack Block so the long brick building runs across your frame with the open ground in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the Barrack Block works as a Victorian backdrop. If the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for brickwork and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the long brick facade level along one of the horizontal lines, with the open ground in the lower third.
card.best_time: There's no fixed time. Morning or late afternoon light usually flatters the red brick best, and the Parade Ground is easier to photograph when it's less busy.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the Parade Ground with the whole Barrack Block behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone offers it, to fit the building over your shoulder. You can also pose against the railings on the footbridge from the Central–Mid-Levels Escalator, which has red and white brick, before you even go in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Parade Ground near Pottinger Gate and shoot towards the Police Headquarters Block, so you and the whole block fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Opening hours can vary and some exhibitions need tickets, so check the official Tai Kwun site on the day.
card.challenge: Get two shots of the same brick wall: one close-up at 2x showing every brick, then one from far back at 1x with you tiny in front of it.
card.good_to_know: Tai Kwun has 16 historic buildings, put up between 1841 and 1925. Victoria Prison was decommissioned in 2006, and the compound reopened on 29 May 2018 as a centre for heritage and arts. Two new buildings were added, with designs inspired by the old brickwork.

card.hook: Hong Kong's tallest building is 484 m of tower, and it's surprisingly hard to photograph well. Give it a statue and a bit of harbour to stand behind and suddenly it looks like a proper postcard.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Avenue of Stars, in the Arena of Stars section. The ICC is to the north-west of here, so turn that way and keep a statue or the promenade rail in front of you, with the harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the statues, the harbour and the tower in one frame. If the tower looks small, try zoom 2x. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the statues big in the foreground, and keep them away from the edges so they don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, with a little sky left above the roof.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, the golden hour, and arrive a bit early to try a few angles before the light changes. After dark, use night mode and hold still until it finishes.
card.selfie_here: The Arena of Stars section of the Avenue of Stars is the best-supported backdrop we've found, especially at sunset. Use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x for a wider shot) and try to get the tower over your shoulder. Check the screen first, because the tower may not be directly behind you from every spot.
card.ask_someone: Around sunset on the Arena of Stars promenade, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame you with the ICC in the background, and check the tower is in the shot before they press the button.
card.rules_and_safety: The Avenue of Stars is a free, open waterfront walk, but check the official site before you go in case sections are closed or changed.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead upright on a gridline, a statue in front, and a strip of sky above the roof. Bonus points if it's the statue's best side.
card.good_to_know: The ICC has 108 storeys, stands 484 m high and was finished in 2010. Its height was scaled back from an earlier plan because buildings weren't allowed to rise above the surrounding mountains. It also hosts a big LED light and music show on two facades, so check locally for show times.

card.hook: The wheel is one big clean circle sitting against open water and sky, so your photo looks tidy without you doing much at all.
card.stand_here: Walk the waterfront from the wheel towards HKCEC for about 600 m to Tamar Park. Then turn round and look back towards Central Pier and the wheel, which sits to the north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole wheel with some harbour around it. If your phone has zoom 2x, try it for a tighter shot of the wheel on its own (higher zooms depend on your phone). Only use 0.5x if you get right up close, like at Central Pier No. 9.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the wheel, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the wheel doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest time on the waterfront. If you want the wheel lit up, wait until after dark and switch on night mode, bracing your elbows against a railing or your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Grab the wooden benches that face the water on the Central Harbourfront promenade, sit or stand by them and put the wheel in the background. Use the front camera and tilt it so the wheel sits over your shoulder. You can also try the waterfront path towards Tamar Park, with the wheel behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on the footbridge towards Jardine House to take your photo from there, but look at the signs first as access may have changed.
card.rules_and_safety: Riding the wheel is ticketed, and access to the footbridge and Central Pier No. 9 may change, so check the signs on the day or the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Put the wheel on one of your vertical gridlines, keep the horizon dead level, and see if you can get a shot where the harbour doesn't slope at all.
card.good_to_know: The wheel is about 60 metres tall and has 42 gondolas. A ride takes about 15 minutes, with two to three turns. It was built on reclaimed land between Central Pier No. 9 and Pier No. 10 and opened in late 2014, then reopened on 20 December 2017 as part of the AIA Vitality Park.

card.hook: Picture a whole city standing on the far side of the water, just waiting for you to lean on a railing and say hello. That's the Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade, and it's one of the easiest skyline shots in Hong Kong.
card.stand_here: Walk west along the harbourfront to the middle section of the Avenue of Stars; it's about 600 m to the west from the harbour edge. Keep the water on your side, then turn to face Hong Kong Island.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view of the railing with the skyline behind it. If the crowd stops you stepping back, try zoom 0.5x. To pick out a group of towers across the water, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the skyline, then drag the slider down so the picture is a little darker and the lit buildings don't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunrise is said to be much quieter on the Avenue of Stars, though the skyline is less lit then. The Symphony of Lights show runs nightly at 8 PM and the waterfront gets very crowded beforehand, so arrive early if you want a spot at the rail.
card.selfie_here: Pose next to the bronze Bruce Lee statue on the Avenue of Stars with the harbour promenade behind you, and expect a short queue for a clear shot. If it's busy, try the waterside railings in the middle of the promenade, facing the Hong Kong Island skyline, and move slightly east toward the museums for more room. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the big 4.5-metre Hong Kong Film Award statuette at the Avenue of Stars entrance and ask a passer-by to frame you against the promenade from the entrance side.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a public harbourfront walkway, but check the official site before you go for any works, closures or event arrangements.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the railing along the lower third, keep the horizon dead level, and see if you can get a friend pointing at the tallest tower without wobbling the skyline.
card.good_to_know: Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade is the railed harbourfront walkway on the Kowloon side of Victoria Harbour. Several guides call the view from the middle of the Avenue of Stars the classic postcard shot. Want a different angle? Try the Tsim Sha Tsui Clock Tower, with its red-brick tower in the foreground, or the eastern end of the promenade, where buildings stacked along the waterfront give a compressed skyline.

card.hook: Most skyscrapers hide their bones. This one wears them on the outside, with big steel masts and triangular trusses holding the whole tower up.
card.stand_here: Head to Statue Square, where the tower is to the south-west, about 184 m away and roughly 3 minutes on foot. Face the entrance across Des Voeux Road Central from the lions.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full front of the tower. If the top gets cut off, try zoom 0.5x and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean in. Zoom 2x or 5x is great for close-ups of the trusses and steel masts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the tower's vertical edges straight, then tap the tower and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at night, when the tower is lit up and the plaza gives you plenty of room. Switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady. Daylight works too, and it shows off the steel structure nicely.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open clearing of Statue Square with your back to the building, so nothing blocks the facade behind you. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if the tower won't fit. For a classic one, pose beside the bronze lions at the entrance with the tower rising over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand inside Charter Garden and frame the whole tower so it all fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the building may be restricted, so shoot from outside and respect any signs you see. The ground floor sometimes hosts exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you keep both sides of the tower dead straight on the gridlines, with a lion tucked in at the bottom of the frame?
card.good_to_know: Norman Foster designed the HSBC Main Building, and it was finished in 1985. It stands 178.8 metres high with 47 storeys. At the time it was the most expensive building in the world, and its steel modules were prefabricated in Britain and shipped to Hong Kong.

card.hook: The Cultural Centre looks like a giant sandy-coloured wave that someone tipped on its side, and it's parked right beside the harbour. Even on a busy day, that curved wall and those leaning pillars stand out against the skyline.
card.stand_here: Stand on Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade, the waterfront stretch beside the Cultural Centre, near the railing. Face Hong Kong Island across the water, so the centre sits off to one side and the harbour fills the rest.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the centre, the harbour and the skyline all in one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the curved wall or a slice of skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line, then tap the bright sky and slide it a touch darker so the lights across the water don't glare.
card.best_time: One guide suggests blue hour, about 15 to 30 minutes after sunset, when the sky goes deep blue and the skyline lights up. The promenade gets very crowded before the nightly Symphony of Lights show, so arrive early to bag a clear spot.
card.selfie_here: Try the open square outside the Cultural Centre, near the long benches by the upper flyover that faces the harbour. A Trip.com guide calls it a good sunset spot, so use the front camera at 0.5x and let the building sit behind your shoulder. Check on the map that it lines up before you commit.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is an open public waterfront, but photography is generally not allowed inside the halls during performances. If you're going inside, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Can you get the leaning pillars, the harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline all in one frame without a stranger's head sneaking in?
card.good_to_know: José Lei designed the centre, and Charles, Prince of Wales and Princess Diana officially opened it on 8 November 1989. It stands on the site of the old Kowloon railway station, and pulling that station down was very controversial at the time. Inside, the 2,019-seat Concert Hall has an 8,000-pipe organ, described as the largest in Asia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade, the waterfront stretch beside the Cultural Centre, near the railing. Face Hong Kong Island across the water, so the centre sits off to one side and the harbour fills the rest.

card.hook: Picture a six-metre gold flower glowing on a deep red base, with Victoria Harbour wide open behind it. That's the shot everyone comes here for, and it's easy to get.
card.stand_here: Walk to the centre of Golden Bauhinia Square, right in front of the statue, and face it so the harbour sits behind it. For a second view, stand on Expo Promenade at the waterfront edge beside the square and face Victoria Harbour towards Kowloon.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue with the harbour behind it. Go 0.5x to fit the whole square and lots of sky, or 2x to 5x for a tighter shot of the flower on its base (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gold of the statue, then slide the brightness a little darker so the gilding keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or near sunset gives you softer light and fewer people. The flag-raising ceremony is around 8 a.m. and draws a crowd, so get there before it starts if you want a clear view of the statue.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the square, in front of the golden bauhinia sculpture, and turn so it's behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the whole statue fits, and hold your phone with both hands because the waterfront can be windy.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't get in the way of the flag-raising ceremony, and don't climb the statues. Some areas may be closed for ceremonies or events, so check the official site before you go. Keep an eye on your belongings.
card.challenge: Line the statue up on one of the vertical gridlines, with just water and sky behind it. Bonus points if it looks as proud as a 'Golden Pak Choi'.
card.good_to_know: The statue stands about six metres high on a red granite base shaped like a pillar on a pyramid. The Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre next door is where the 1997 handover ceremonies were held, so it means a lot to many people in Hong Kong. Locals have nicknamed it the "Golden Pak Choi". Some visitors report vendors near the statue offering paid photos. You can politely ignore them and take your own.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the centre of Golden Bauhinia Square, right in front of the statue, and face it so the harbour sits behind it. For a second view, stand on Expo Promenade at the waterfront edge beside the square and face Victoria Harbour towards Kowloon.

card.hook: Central is all glass and steel, and then there's a small grey Gothic church tucked among the trees like it missed the memo. It's the best kind of surprise in this part of town.
card.stand_here: Stand on Garden Road opposite the cathedral, by the Peak Tram lower terminus. The cathedral is to the north-east, about 200 m away from the terminus (a few minutes on foot), so face north-east and you'll see the whole building across the road with the grounds and trees in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the cathedral across the road. If trees or traffic push you in close, switch to zoom 0.5x. Try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the bell tower and its big "VR".
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical grid line, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Avoid service times and wedding slots, because the cathedral is an active place of worship and weddings are held often. Check the cathedral's website for events before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the courtyard just outside the main entrance, then turn so the building is behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the Gothic front into your selfie.
card.ask_someone: Try handing your phone to someone on the Garden Road pavement by the bus stop directly in front of the cathedral, so they can frame the whole facade with you in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't use flash, and don't photograph during services. Weddings and services happen here, so check the event schedule first, and don't disturb anyone praying in the small prayer room.
card.challenge: Spot the big "VR" on the bell tower and the Celtic memorial cross, then get both into one photo.
card.good_to_know: St John's was consecrated in 1852 and is the oldest surviving Western church building in Hong Kong. It was declared a monument in 1996. The style is a plain version of 13th-century English Gothic, and the "VR" on the bell tower stands for Queen Victoria.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Garden Road opposite the cathedral, by the Peak Tram lower terminus.
